newsitem.title: FRANCE: McQueen triumphs with no-bones Givenchy couture.
newsitem.headline: McQueen triumphs with no-bones Givenchy couture.

text.p: Make no bones about it: Alexander McQueen sent out an extraordinary haute couture collection for Givenchy, blending Oriental, Spanish and British influences in a dramatic fashion spectacle that brought the house down.
But contrary to pre-show rumours there were no bones. At least not human ones.

With this show, Britain's nasty boy disproved the naysayers who had panned his first collection for the once staid fashion label, crafting a beautifully tailored and staged parade mixing both theatrical and serious clothes.

Bird skulls perched on the shoulders of a leather dress, and a foxhead drooped over a model's forehead. From the feather bustier of a magnificent bustled lace gown, the neck of a goose wound its way around the neck of supermodel Shalom Harlow.

The animal paraphernalia, including feather headdresses, crocodile jackets and snakeskin inserts on crepe jumpsuits was paraded alongside the striking S-curve of a Belle Epoque gown or the overly swollen sleeves of a black Victorian dress -- slashed and ruffled at the knee above stiletto heeled ankle boots.

Supermodels towered in six-inch (15 cm) platform shoes and gigantic hairdos -- mimmicking Star Wars Pricess Leia or an Edwardian maiden, as crows fluttered nervously in the Paris medical faculty halls carpeted with bear- and tiger-skin rugs.

A golden dragon richly embroidered on a Chinese ceremonial robe, Scottish plaids cinched tight on the body with wide swooping sleeves brimming with Spanish lace, toreador boleros decked with tassles, jewels and leopard skin trim: the show was a masterpiece mixing theatrics and serious clothes.
One model had her head submerged in a Belle Epoque gown with a caged bird in its place, another had eyes dyed bright orange to match a macrame bonnet.

The collection was a relief for the fashion crowd, which had been up in arms over a Sunday Times article asserting that the subversive 28-year-old son of a taxi driver had sewn human body parts, including teeth and bones, into Givenchy's clothes.

"He is very controversial, a real provocateur, but he wouldn't be that crazy," said Nicole Fischlis, vice president of the U.S. department store Saks Fifth Avenue. "What it certainly contains is the sweat from the petite mains (seamstresses) who worked on it."
Fischelis said McQueen, hired at Givenchy in October, was attracting a new clientele to the house which had long catered to prim and mature customers.
If McQueen had chosen the macabre theme, it would not have been the first time he shocked his audience.

As an apprentice in men's tailoring on London's Savile Row, he chalked obscenities inside a jacket made for the Prince of Wales, and for his own London-based collection, he splattered crushed insects on garments and lined coats with human hair.

But McQueen's controversial, high profile is one of the main reasons he was hired at Givenchy -- to give a strong brand image to sell the label's more lucrative spin-off products like perfume, cosmetics and accessories.
Earlier, Olivier Lapidus delivered a collection he said was adorned and embroidered "diamond dust, micro-rubies and emerald fragments".

But aside from the sparkles strewn across an evening gown and hand-painted diamond motifs on an A-line mini, the "innovation" and "totally new approach" announced in the press packet was nowhere to be seen.
More truthfully, Lapidus presented some little black cocktail numbers of crepe georgette and chiffon, splashy print coats and trouser suits of iridescent silk.
